list.listitem: Suspect anthrax when there have been several cases of acute febrile illness that follow a fulminant course and lead to high death rates, and in patients with acute febrile illness following a specific bioterrorism attack. Among farm workers, outbreaks may be preceded by livestock deaths. B

Approximately 70% of patients with inhalation anthrax will have an infiltrate, widened mediastinum, pleural effusion, or mediastinal adenopathy on chest imaging.
B

Anthrax is confirmed by direct testing for Bacillus anthracis in blood, skin lesion swab, spinal fluid or respiratory secretions taken prior to antibiotic administration or by measuring antibodies or toxin in blood. A

Patients with systemic anthrax should initially receive multiple IV antibiotics to include at least one bactericidal agent PLUS a protein synthesis inhibitor. If meningitis is suspected, possible or confirmed, administer 2 bactericidal agents PLUS a protein synthesis inhibitor should be administered. C
The CDC recommends antitoxin treatments in cases of systemic anthrax; however, it is unknown whether they confer benefit to patients treated with antimicrobials. C
An antitoxin should be added to the combination antimicrobial treatment for patients for whom there is a high level of suspicion for systemic anthrax. C
Glucocorticoid treatment for 2-3 weeks should be considered for anthrax meningitis in accordance with the protocols for bacterial meningitis. C

After the initial parenteral therapy, the patient can be switched to monotherapy (oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily) to complete a total of 60 days of treatment. C

background.definition: Anthrax is an infectious disease caused by Bacillus anthracis, a Gram-positive, spore-forming rod. Anthrax infection occurs by 3 routes: inhalational, GI, and cutaneous.

list.listitem: No cases of anthrax were reported in the United States in 2005. A case of inhalation anthrax was reported in 2006 and 2 cases of cutaneous anthrax in 2007 from exposure to dried animal hides in the making of traditional African drums. In 2009, a case of gastrointestinal anthrax was reported from exposure through drumming on an animal-hide drum. One case was reported to the CDC in 2019 from Texas.
Among heroin users, 52 new anthrax cases were reported in the United Kingdom and 3 in Germany in 2009-2010.

In a study from Georgia, the incidence of anthrax was highest in peri-urban areas at 24.5 cases per 1 million population which was greater than 3-fold higher than in urban and 2-fold higher than in rural areas. The authors believe that this finding was due to an increased risk from handling or purchasing contaminated meat and meat by-products.

Based on a newspaper article, an anthrax outbreak occurred in 2016 when 72 nomadic herders in the Arctic Circle were hospitalized and one child died. This outbreak was linked to warming temperatures uncovering an anthrax-infected reindeer carcass and killing several thousand reindeer.

Two outbreaks of anthrax occurred in Ethiopia in 2018-2019. In the first outbreak, 49 cows died of suspected anthrax, 22 people developed symptoms consistent with cutaneous anthrax (40% attack rate), 3 were confirmed as having anthrax based on real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing, and two died of suspected anthrax ingestion. In the second outbreak, anthrax was suspected to have caused the deaths of two livestock animals, 18 people had suspected cutaneous anthrax (27% attack rate), and one person died. Although none of the 12 human samples collected from the second outbreak tested positive for anthrax by PCR, a swab taken from the dried meat of one animal case (goat) was positive.
Of the biological agents that might be used as weapons, anthrax is one of the most serious and could infect large populations.
Caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis, a Gram-positive, spore-forming rod.
Anthrax occurs naturally in soil. Humans contract anthrax spores from contact with anthrax-infected animals or anthrax-contaminated animal products or animal feed.
Anthrax can also be spread through bioterrorism, and laboratory workers can contract it by exposure.
The risk of anthrax and other spore-forming bacteria (e.g., botulism, tetanus, Clostridium novyi) is increased in persons who inject drugs.

When inhaled, ingested, or inoculated, anthrax spores are deposited in tissues where some are destroyed by macrophages. The remaining spores are transported lymphatically to local or regional lymph nodes where they germinate. Activation of spores typically occurs in 1 to 6 days but can take up to 60 days.
The replicating B. anthracis then release lethal toxins that cause hemorrhage, tissue damage, liver damage, and pleural edema.
Once toxin levels reach a critical threshold, death occurs even if the bacilli are eradicated with antibiotics.

Authors of a systematic review of 931 patients hospitalized with anthrax found a median incubation period of 1 day (interquartile range [IQR], 0-4) for injection to 7 days (IQR, 4-9) for inhalation anthrax.

If using animal hides, risk is lower if coming from animals from the United States or that were imported with an international veterinary certificate showing that they have undergone appropriate government inspection. C
Masks used when processing animal hair appear protective.

The acellular anthrax vaccine Anthrax Vaccine Absorbed (AVA, brand name BioThrax) is recommended for laboratory and agricultural workers at high risk of exposure; some people who handle animals or animal products, such as veterinarians who handle infected animals; and for selected military personnel at risk of exposure. C

While usually given subcutaneously, the vaccine may be given intramuscularly if the subcutaneous route of administration poses significant challenges during an emergency that might delay or preclude vaccination.

For pre-exposure prophylaxis, AVA is given as a 6-dose primary series (at 0, 2, and 4 weeks, and at 6, 12, and 18 months) with annual boosters. C In the 2019 update from the US Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, a booster can be given every 3 years instead of annually to persons not at high risk for exposure to Bacillus anthracis who have previously received the initial anthrax vaccine absorbed 3-dose priming and 2-dose booster series and want to maintain protection.

The vaccine is associated with minor side effects (myalgias, arthralgias, headache, and fatigue) in 8% of patients after the first dose and decreasing rates of side effects with successive doses. It is contraindicated in patients with previous infection or anaphylaxis with previous immunization. B

Vaccination against anthrax does not appear to be associated with long-term disability among US Army Veterans or adverse effects on health-related quality of life at 30 months among voluntary vaccine recipients. B

Another vaccine, Anthrax Vaccine Precipitated (AVP), which has a 4-dose primary series is used in the UK. A recent study found optimal timing for a booster dose was well over 2 years for improved serologic response prompting a change in vaccine recommendations from UK anthrax vaccination guidelines, extending the interval between routine AVP boosters from one to 10 years.

A plant-derived recombinant protective antigen (rPA)-based vaccine against Bacillus anthracis underwent phase 1 testing and was found to be safe and immunogenic at all 4 dose levels, with no vaccine-related serious adverse events observed.
After exposure, vaccination alone is ineffective, but the CDC recommends its use in combination with antibiotics. B

Prophylactic management of known or suspected inhalation exposure to anthrax is with oral ciprofloxacin or doxycycline for 60 days (the longest germination time of inhaled spores) and a three-dose series of anthrax vaccine over 4 weeks. C

Work is underway on developing a two-dose vaccination for post-exposure prophylaxis. Phase 1 trial data on 54 healthy subjects showed that the vaccine, administered as two IM doses 28 days apart, elicited a protective antibody response starting at seven days after the second vaccination and was well-tolerated.

Authors of a systematic review of 12 publications and 2 case reports conducted in rabbits and nonhuman primates found all 3 FDA-approved anthrax antitoxins demonstrated significant improvement in survival as monotherapy over placebo. Limited data are available through case reports on antitoxin use in humans. Based on data from 25 patients with systemic anthrax disease treated with antitoxins, 17 survived.
Administration of the anti-toxin raxibacumab with anthrax vaccination does not negatively affect vaccine immunogenicity.

Suspect anthrax when there have been several cases of acute febrile illness that follow a fulminant course and lead to high death rates, and in patients with acute febrile illness following a specific bioterrorism attack or use of animal hides. C
The median time from exposure to developing symptoms is approximately 4 days. B

Anthrax is confirmed by direct testing for Bacillus anthracis in blood, skin lesion swab, spinal fluid or respiratory secretions taken prior to antibiotic administration or by measuring antibodies or toxin in blood. A
Approximately 70% of patients with inhalation anthrax will have infiltrates, widened mediastinums, pleural effusions, or mediastinal adenopathy on chest imaging. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Cultures positive for different organisms; mediastinum not widened

list.listitem: Suspect cutaneous anthrax in patients with an exposure history who have localized itching followed by a papular lesion that turns vesicular and develops a black eschar within 7-10 days of the initial lesion.

Suspect inhalation anthrax in patients with an exposure history who have symptoms of respiratory infection and develop abrupt onset of high fever and severe respiratory distress (dyspnea, stridor, cyanosis).

A checklist to distinguish patients with anthrax from those with other conditions has been developed and validated. In the event of possible anthrax exposure, the checklist recommends immediate IV therapy for any person with heart rate >110 bpm, respiratory rate >20 breaths/minute, new confusion, or severe headache.

Suspect anthrax meningitis in patients with systemic anthrax who have two or more of the following—severe headaches, altered mental status including confusion, meningeal signs, or other neurological symptoms/signs. In patients with systemic disease, meningitis occurs in about half.

Suspect GI anthrax in patients with nausea, vomiting, malaise, bloody diarrhea, and acute abdominal pain after consuming potentially contaminated meat. After 2-4 days, ascites develops in more than half of patients as abdominal pain decreases.

Suspect oropharyngeal anthrax in a patient with an exposure history and fever, throat pain, dysphagia, ulcers at the base of the tongue that become necrotic and marked unilateral or bilateral regional lymphadenopathy.
In the bioterrorism attacks of 2001, the median time from exposure to developing symptoms was 4 days (range = 4-6 days).

Among the first 10 victims, all reported fever and chills, all had fatigue or malaise, 7 had sweats, 9 had minimal or nonproductive cough, 8 had dyspnea, and 9 had nausea or vomiting. Clinically, 7 of these patients had fever greater than 37.8°C (100°F) and 8 had a heart rate faster than 100 beats per minute.
Altered mental status is also common and helps distinguish patients with anthrax poisoning from those with community-acquired pneumonia.

Anthrax is confirmed by direct testing for Bacillus anthracis in blood, skin lesion swab, spinal fluid or respiratory secretions taken prior to antibiotic administration. The disease can also be confirmed by measuring antibodies or toxin in blood. Samples are sent for culture and PCR testing or a serum sample can be obtained to test for anthrax lethal factor toxin. The acute sample is sent ≤7 days after symptom onset OR as soon as possible after a known exposure event and convalescent sample 14-35 days after symptom onset.
The WBC in the victims of the 2001 attacks was not very discriminating: the median count was 9800 per mL (range = 7500-13,300). A hematocrit level greater than 45% is associated with anthrax.
None of the victims had elevated serum transaminases; 6 were hypoxic. In a more recent review of 13 U.S. hospital cases of inhalation anthrax from 2001-2011, 9 of 11 had elevated transaminases.
Of 8 patients in one case series who had blood cultures performed before starting antibiotics, all 8 grew Bacillus species.
In the anthrax attacks of 2001, each of the first 10 patients had abnormal chest x-ray results: 7 with infiltrates, 7 with widened mediastinum, and 8 with pleural effusion.
In addition, 8 of the patients had chest CT scans and 7 showed mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
The CDC recommends lumbar puncture for patients with systemic anthrax to determine whether they have anthrax meningitis, provided that no contraindications exist.
Although the experience with cutaneous and GI anthrax is more limited, direct culture of vesicles or fecal material is recommended.
Confirmatory tests such as immunohistochemical staining, gamma phage, and PCR assays must be performed by special reference laboratories.
Detailed instructions, including packaging and shipping information by specimen and test type, are available on CDC website.

A point-of-care test using blood sample processing and PCR amplification for B. anthracis read on a GeneXpert instrument appears to be highly sensitive. In addition, a mass spectrometry method for quantification of anthrax lethal factor, a zinc-dependent endoprotease and critical virulence factor, also appears to be highly sensitive and specific allowing for early diagnosis and evaluation of treatment. Other point-of-care tests are under development.

Dried blood spot matrix assay method using quantitative anti-protective antigen IgG enzyme-linked immunosorbent (ELISA) assay may be an alternative to serum testing and is associated with fewer on-site equipment requirements and lower storage and transport costs. This ELISA assay has been validated for serological diagnosis of anthrax infection in the field and for diagnosis of cutaneous anthrax.

A classification and regression tree algorithm was developed on the basis of 47 known cases of laboratory and bioterror exposure to anthrax compared with 188 matched control cases with community-acquired pneumonia.

A checklist was developed for initial triage after an anthrax mass exposure event and tested using published cases of 408 patients with inhalation, ingestion, and cutaneous anthrax and primary anthrax meningitis, and 657 control patients. The checklist contained 2 parts - a paramedical evaluation for tachypnea >20 breaths per minute, tachycardia >110 bpm, altered mental status, or severe headache followed by a medical assessment for those who had any tachycardia (>100-109 bpm), fever, diaphoresis, or dyspnea looking for the presence of abnormal lung sounds, increasing abdominal girth, or characteristic skin lesions. Checklist-directed triage without diagnostic testing correctly classified 95% (95% CI, 93% to 97%) of 353 adult anthrax case patients and 76% (CI, 73% to 79%) of 647 control patients (positive LR 3.96 [95%CI 3.45-4.55]; negative LR 0.07 [95% CI 0.04 to 0.11]; false-negative rate 5%; false-positive rate 24%). Patients who had exposure but none of these signs or symptoms would receive post-exposure prophylactic treatment with instructions to follow-up if symptoms develop.

Authors of a systematic review of 10 triage algorithms for different bioterrorism situations note that it is necessary to determine the time and place of the attack as soon as possible, control the number of exposed and potentially exposed people, prevent infection and determine the type of biological agents used. For anthrax, there is a need to improve the distinction between inhalational anthrax symptoms and common disease symptoms.

A 4-item screening tool for presence of meningitis in patients with systemic anthrax was developed using a literature review of 363 anthrax cases of whom 36% met anthrax meningitis criteria. Presence on admission of any one of severe headache, altered mental status, meningeal signs, or other neurological signs had a sensitivity for anthrax meningitis of 89% and 83% in the adult and pediatric validation cohorts. Presence of 2 or more made meningitis highly likely (positive likelihood ratio 26.5 and 30 for adults and children, respectively). Anthrax meningitis was unlikely in the absence of any of these signs or symptoms (negative likelihood ratio 0.12 and 0.19 for adults and children, respectively).

Authors assessing single or paired algorithms for identifying meningitis among patients with systemic anthrax found that use of a single algorithm with 1 or more neurological symptoms or signs achieved high sensitivity (86%, 95% CI 71%-100%) and specificity (90%, 95% CI 82%-98%). Pairing algorithms with the same symptoms and signs improved specificity (99%, 95% CI 97%-100%), but left 17.3% of patients in an indeterminate meningitis category and pairing algorithms with differing symptoms and signs only slightly improved specificity over the single algorithm (92%, 95% CI 85%-99%).

Among patients with cough, congestion, and dyspnea consistent with community-acquired pneumonia, those with the following were at high risk for inhalation anthrax: (1) an altered mental status and a chest x-ray that showed mediastinal widening or (2) no mediastinal widening but a hematocrit level greater than 45%.
Public health officials are encouraged to develop a local protocol for screened individuals in need of prophylactic antibiotics in case of an anthrax event.
Patients with known exposure and respiratory symptoms should be hospitalized; no respiratory isolation is required.
Blood cultures and other body fluid cultures are the key to diagnosis.
Empiric treatment with ciprofloxacin plus doxycycline before definitive diagnosis is recommended for all patients.
Suspected or confirmed anthrax cases should be reported immediately to the local or state Department of Health.
Patients with systemic anthrax and suspected, possible, or confirmed meningitis should receive 2 bactericidal agents PLUS a protein synthesis inhibitor., C

An antitoxin should be added to the combination antimicrobial treatment for patients for whom there is a high level of suspicion for systemic anthrax. C Clinical data on efficacy are based on non-human studies of poor quality but show some benefit on survival.
Patients with inhalation anthrax should initially receive multiple antibiotics to include at least one bactericidal agent PLUS a protein synthesis inhibitor. C

After the initial parenteral therapy, the patient can be switched to monotherapy (oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily) to complete a total of 60 days of treatment. C

Patients with uncomplicated cutaneous anthrax can be treated with a single oral antibiotic (ciprofloxacin or doxycycline or penicillin for penicillin-sensitive isolates) for 6-10 days. In an intentional attack, treatment is extended to 60 days. C
There are no clinical trials for the treatment of anthrax and most therapeutic recommendations are based on animal studies.

The CDC (2015) recommends multiple drugs for the initial treatment of systemic anthrax. If meningitis is suspected, possible or confirmed, use two bactericidal agents—a fluoroquinolone and a ß-lactam—PLUS one protein synthesis inhibitor. Choices include IV ciprofloxicin or levofloxacin or moxifloxacin PLUS meropenem or imipenem or doripenem PLUS linezolid or chloramphenicol., Rifampin can be used rather than one of the protein synthesis inhibitors. For penicillin-susceptible strains, penicillin G or ampicillin can be substituted for the ß-lactam.

If meningitis has been excluded, patients with systemic anthrax should be treated with a single bactericidal agent PLUS a protein synthesis inhibitor. Choices include ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin or moxifloxacin or meropenem or imipenem or doripenem or vancomycin PLUS linezolid or clindamycin or doxycycline. Rifampin can be used rather than one of the protein synthesis inhibitors. For penicillin-susceptible strains, penicillin G or ampicillin can be substituted as the bactericidal agent.

In a systematic review of 123 cases of non-cutaneous severe anthrax, those receiving combination bactericidal and protein synthesis inhibitor therapy had a 45% survival compared to 28% survival in the absence of combination therapy. For cases with meningitis, survival was greater for those receiving 3 or more antimicrobials compared to 1 or 2 antimicrobials (3 of 4 [75%] vs. 12 of 73 [16%], respectively).

In a more recent systematic review of 605 hospitalized patients with anthrax including 430 adults, 145 children, and 30 missing age, most patients with localized cutaneous or non-meningitis systemic anthrax survived with 1 or more antimicrobials. However, survival of patients with inhalation anthrax without meningitis was better with at least 2 antimicrobials. In this study, neither the addition of a protein synthesis inhibitor(s) or antitoxin/antiserum to bactericidal antimicrobials improved survival among those with systemic anthrax. Mannitol but not steroids improved survival for patients with meningitis. Finally, antimicrobial postexposure prophylaxis reduced risk of anthrax following exposure to B. anthracis.
Patients with inhalation anthrax should receive multiple antibiotics to include at least one bactericidal agent PLUS a protein synthesis inhibitor.

Patients with cutaneous anthrax can be treated with a single oral antibiotic for 6-10 days (ciprofloxacin or doxycycline); duration of treatment is extended to 60 days if there is concern about risk of inhaled anthrax.
Penicillin is the first choice for naturally-acquired GI anthrax. Ciprofloxacin is a second option.
Glucocorticoid treatment for 2-3 weeks should be considered for anthrax meningitis in accordance with the protocols for bacterial meningitis.

Three FDA-approved antitoxins are available: raxibacumab, anthrax immune globulin, and obiltoxaximab. The CDC recommends antitoxin treatments in cases of systemic anthrax; however, it is unknown whether they confer benefit to patients treated with antimicrobials.

Based on data from 3 clinical trials including 322 healthy subjects, a dose of 40 mg/kg raxibacumab provided comparable exposure across all subjects, with some variation based on weight. For children, authors of a modeling study suggest use of a weight-banded dosing regimen of 75 mg/kg for individuals ≤1.5 kg, 55 mg/kg for individuals <10 kg, 45 mg/kg for individuals <50 kg, and 40 mg/kg for all individuals >50 kg.

For inhalation anthrax, the FDA approved obiltoxaximab (ETI-204, 2018), a toxin-targeting monoclonal antibody, intravenously to use in combination with antibacterial drugs. This drug is similar to raxibacumab. Oblitoxaximab can also be used for prophylaxis of inhalational anthrax when other therapies are unavailable or inappropriate. Adverse effects reported in 320 healthy volunteers included a hypersensitivity reaction in 34 (10.6%) with anaphylaxis in 3 subjects.

After the initial parenteral therapy, if the patient is clinically stable, he or she can be switched to monotherapy with either oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily.
The total duration of therapy (parenteral and oral) should be 60 days.
In the 2001 attacks, 7 of the patients needed drainage of pleural effusions, 3 with chest tubes.
Adjunctive therapies, including drainage of pleural effusions, ascites, and pericardial effusions, all of which are toxin-laden, may help reduce mortality.
Many patients with cutaneous anthrax will develop eschars that require debridement.
All patients with inhalational anthrax symptoms should be hospitalized.

Information regarding medical countermeasure use during an anthrax-mass casualty incident including hospital-based acute care with antitoxins and intravenous antimicrobial use and diagnosis and management of common anthrax-specific complications is available from the CDC.
The anthrax attacks of 2001 resulted in 11 cases of inhalational anthrax, resulting in 5 deaths. B

Mortality rates for untreated disease are estimated at up to 60% for GI anthrax, 34% for injection-related anthrax, and 45%-90% for inhalation anthrax. B Authors of a systematic review including 764 adults and 167 children globally, found mortality rates of 31% for cutaneous to 90% for primary meningitis since 1960.

In a systematic review, the mortality rate was 4% for the 26 patients with cutaneous anthrax with only systemic inflammatory response syndrome and 76% among the 33 patients with cutaneous anthrax complicated by meningitis. The overall mortality rate for the 123 cases of more severe anthrax was 67%. B
Even without antibiotic therapy, the mortality rate for uncomplicated cutaneous anthrax is generally less than 1%; with appropriate antibiotic treatment, death is rare. B

Authors of a systematic review including182 patients of whom 47 (25.8%) died found the following risk factors predictive of death or meningitis: fever or chills, nausea or vomiting, headache, leukocytosis, bacteremia, anxiety, abdominal pain, diastolic hypotension, skin trauma, thoracic edema, malignant pustule edema, lymphadenopathy, and evidence of coagulopathy.

Inadvertent vaccination against anthrax in the first trimester vs. later in pregnancy did not confer higher risk of birth defects among military women, although there was a slightly higher risk of birth defects with vaccination prepregnancy vs. postpregnancy (OR 1.11; 95% CI 1.01-1.22).

In a systematic review of anthrax during pregnancy, 20 cases were identified. Seventeen were infected pregnant women, two contracted anthrax postpartum, and one case was in a lactating woman. Sixteen women died and 12 fetal or neonatal losses were reported. Most cases occurred prior to the availability of antibiotics.

Although fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines should not typically be used in pregnant women, animal studies have demonstrated low teratogenicity and the potential catastrophic outcomes of inadequately treated anthrax are sufficient to offset these concerns.
Clinical disease in children appears to be like adults.

Treatment in children is like recommended treatment in adults. Although fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines should not typically be used in children, the potential catastrophic outcomes of inadequately treated anthrax are sufficient to offset these concerns.

A Pediatric Preparedness Resource Kit, developed by the American Academy of Pediatrics, is available to facilitate partnerships and joint decision-making between clinicians and state and/or local health departments.
